newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: ABARE sees steady A$ despite commodity price rise.
newsitem.headline: ABARE sees steady A$ despite commodity price rise.

text.p: The Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) said on Tuesday it expected the Australian dollar to hold at an average of US$0.78 over 1997/98 despite expected higher commodity prices.

ABARE, the Australian government's main commodities forecaster, said it was assuming that interest rate differentials between Australia and major overseas economies would continue to narrow in the short-term.

The prices of Australian-produced commodities on world markets were forecast to recover moderately in 1997/98 to June 30, ABARE said. However, the narrowing of interest rate differentials was likely to limit any upward pressure on the Australian dollar from improved commodity prices, it said.

A 0.5 point cut in Australian rates to 5.5 percent in May brought official rates down to U.S. levels for the first time since the early 1980s and saw the dollar weaken from 78 cents to under 75 cents at present.
ABARE forecast a continued short-term strengthening in Australia's economic growth to an annualised 3.8 percent in 1997/98 from an estimated 3.2 percent in 1996/97.

This follows a strengthening in early 1997, when seasonally adjusted growth in the March quarter occurred at an annualised rate of 3.7 percent. This compared with 1.5 percent in the December quarter and 3.2 percent in the September quarter.

This differs from the method used by the Australian Bureau of Statistics which uses a year-to measure of adding four quarters growth together. This measure saw annual growth slow to 2.4 percent in Q1 this year from 3.1 percent in Q4 1996.
Inflationary pressures were likely to stay low in the short term with headline inflation assumed to average 1.2 percent in 1997/98 against an estimated 1.3 percent in 1996/97, ABARE said.

Excluding mortgage interest and consumer credit charges, the inflation rate was assumed to average a steady 2.3 percent in 1997/98, it said. The Treasury measure of underlying inflation stood at an annual 2.1 percent in the March quarter.
ABARE has also assumed that prime lending rates will remain around the current low level in the short-term to average around 8.8 percent in 1997/98, against 9.8 percent in 1996/97.
